extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, journalists, policymakers interested in misinformation and Sri Lanka
extracted.subtask_description: A topical encyclopedic overview of coordinated fake-news campaigns targeting Muslim-linked businesses after the 2019 Easter bombings in Sri Lanka, including tactics, actors, impacts, corporate and state responses. Useful for understanding patterns of misinformation, responses by firms/platforms/government, and case studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactics used in fake-news campaigns targeting businesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Coordinated social media and trade-level fake news campaigns created hundreds of fake profiles, pages, and content claiming Muslim business funding for terrorists and calling for the boycott of Muslim businesses and their products; posts urged Sinhala consumers to patronise only 'Sinhala' businesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include doctored images, fabricated ownership/transaction narratives, posts recording a monk chasing customers out of a Muslim-owned shop, and targeted false rumours spread via social media and instant messengers (e.g., claims that 'PickMe owner is an ISIS-funder'). These are indicators of an organized misinformation campaign rather than isolated false posts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of fake news on security and economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake news and misinformation contributed to panic and reciprocal attacks: mobs attacked households and businesses, causing at least one death and the destruction of businesses (e.g., a large pasta factory in Minuwangoda); authorities imposed curfews and deployed the army.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor for real-world harm (violence, property destruction, economic boycotts, social discrimination) as key measures of the severity of misinformation campaigns. The article links such harm to calls for boycotts and incitement spread online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical context and actors enabling campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Ultranationalist elements and groups (notably Bodu Bala Sena) have previously spread hate speech and targeted Muslim-linked businesses (going back to 2012), and divisive figures sought to aggravate the situation for political aims after the attacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing misinformation targeting businesses, consider prior activity by extremist/ultranationalist actors and whether campaigns are part of longer-term patterns rather than one-off incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of pre-existing hate speech and post-attack escalation
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media trends showed hate speech was already a prominent topic before the attacks, with an exponential increase in volume of fake news targeting Muslim-linked businesses after the Easter attacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Baseline analysis of hate-speech volume and topic prevalence before and after triggering events helps distinguish opportunistic spikes versus chronic harassment; volume spikes post-event signal coordinated amplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate responses to misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Affected companies publicly condemned fake campaigns, held press conferences to correct manipulated images and false claims, and clarified ownership/board details to dispel allegations (e.g., PickMe chairman's statement; Atlas Axillia's MD raising awareness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporate corrective actions (public statements, disclosure of facts about ownership/board, media engagement) are documented mitigation strategies; effectiveness can be gauged by uptake of corrections and whether harmful rumours are retracted or removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform and international responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Social platforms (Facebook) removed fake profiles/groups/pages, took action against accounts spreading misinformation, and engaged with Sri Lankan authorities; international organisations and watchdogs condemned the inciteful fake news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platform moderation (removals, stricter enforcement) and cooperation with authorities are primary non-legal remedies. Record whether platforms take action, meet authorities, and publicly report enforcement steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and policy responses by the state
rubrics_metrics.description: The government temporarily blocked access to social media to prevent mob coordination and, in June 2019, the Cabinet approved amendments to the Penal Code and Criminal Procedure Code to include spreading of hate speech and fake news as punishable offences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess policy responses by scope (temporary blocks vs new criminal offences), timing (immediate shutdowns vs later legal amendments), and potential impacts on freedom of expression and public safety. Note official claims (e.g., blocks were to prevent mob coordination) when evaluating justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting patterns: religious/ethnic profiling and economic boycotts
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaigns singled out businesses deemed to be owned by Muslims (including firms with halal certification) and spread narratives that Muslims were buying Sinhala businesses and using profits to fund terrorists, leading to merchant threats, school-level discrimination against students using targeted products, and calls for boycotts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for patterns of economic exclusion (boycott calls), product stigmatization (e.g., halal certification as a trigger), and downstream social discrimination (students ridiculed) as hallmarks of identity-based targeting in misinformation campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documented case studies and exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific companies were repeatedly targeted, notably PickMe (ride-hailing app) with fabricated funding claims and doctored images, and Atlas Axillia/Hemas (stationery/conglomerate) with false narratives about Muslim takeover and ensuing merchant and school-level reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific cases to trace the lifecycle of false claims (origin, amplification channels, platform takedown, corporate response, and societal impact). Case studies provide concrete evidence for broader claims about tactics and harms.
